section_1.title: The Analogy: How We Learn from Mistakes
section_1.content: Establish the intuition: Learning is the process of adjusting internal 'settings' to reduce the gap between prediction and reality. Introduce the concept of a 'Loss Function' as a scoreboard for error.
section_1.example: An archer shooting at a target. If the arrow hits too high, the archer adjusts their aim (weights) downward for the next shot to minimize the distance to the bullseye (loss).

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Computational Graph
section_2.content: Visualize the neural network as a flow of information. Nodes represent operations; edges represent weights. Emphasize that every output is a function of the previous layers' inputs.
section_2.example: A chain of dominoes. If you tilt the first one, it triggers a sequence. To change the final result, you must adjust the position of specific dominoes in the chain.

section_3.title: The Gradient: The Direction of Correction
section_3.content: Explain that the 'gradient' acts like a compass. It tells us how much a tiny change in a specific weight will increase or decrease the final error. We use partial derivatives to see the sensitivity.
section_3.example: Standing on a foggy mountain (Error landscape). You cannot see the bottom, but you can feel the slope under your feet. The gradient points in the steepest upward direction; you walk in the opposite direction.

section_4.title: Backpropagation: The Credit Assignment Problem
section_4.content: The core mechanism. We start at the error (the output) and work backward, applying the Chain Rule. We distribute the 'blame' for the error back to each weight based on its contribution.
section_4.example: A cooking line in a restaurant. If a dish tastes too salty, the head chef (Loss) tells the saucier, who tells the prep cook who measured the salt. Each person gets a 'blame' score proportional to their impact on the final taste.

section_5.title: The Loop: Iterative Optimization
section_5.content: Summarize the full cycle: Forward Pass (predict) -> Loss Calculation (measure) -> Backpropagation (calculate gradients) -> Update (adjust weights). This creates an iterative cycle towards intelligence.
section_5.example: A robot learning to recognize a cat: After 1,000 images, the weight adjustments make the robot's internal features 'fire' specifically when it sees whiskers or pointed ears, effectively 'learning' the concept of a cat.
